notes.claim: LIRA is based on transmission line theory: it estimates and analyses the complex line impedance as a function of signal frequency, and measures the surge impedance over a wide range of frequencies.
Your notes say LIRA needs access to only one end, works on frequency-domain resonance effects of unmatched lines, and is sensitive to small changes in insulation permittivity.
Changes in dielectric permittivity change the cable impedance. A damaged segment differs mainly through a change in cable capacitance.

Joints, splices or defects create a deviation in the input impedance spectrum. The resonance frequencies give the cable length and the phase spectrum shows condition and locates joints and degradation.
Wirescan's patent gives the relative phase velocity from two consecutive resonance frequencies: vr = 2L(fk+1 − fk)/v0, where L is the length of the cable and v0 is the speed of light.
LIRA works with any termination except an exact match to the cable impedance, which makes the cable look endless.
DNORM indicates the severity of local impedance changes, and its sign helps determine the type of change.
DNORM normalises the spike difference from the terminal peak, and a local spot has a mirror image beyond the terminal peak from a second-order reflection.

Your notes give a negative DNORM for thermal degradation, water penetration and mechanical causes, and positive for bends and breaks in the shield. Colours run green mild, amber intermediate, red significant.
Your notes say tests are normally bi-directional, take about a minute each, run to 18 tests of core to screen and core to core, have no acceptance criteria, and need the raw trace data kept.
Wirescan's patent says LIRA can estimate the location of a degraded spot to within 0.5% of the cable length.
Both ends are earthed and discharged before a LIRA test so no energy is stored in the cable.

An open-ended line looks like a capacitor at low frequency, then resonates: the input impedance swings between a short and an open at frequencies set by length and velocity, spaced v divided by 2L apart (a quarter wavelength gives a short, a half wavelength an open).

A frequency sweep cannot say where a mismatch is by itself; transforming the reflection data from frequency to distance does. Reflections from a mismatch show as a ripple on the frequency response, and the Fourier transform of the reflection coefficient against frequency gives it against distance.

LIRA's patent finds each reflection's place from the power spectrum of the impedance after a transform: x = vr v0 f'' divided by 2, where f'' is the component in the transformed domain; the sweep runs from 0 to X MHz where X depends on the cable length; Wirescan's FAQ gives 5 000 to 30 000 discrete frequencies per sweep. The lesson uses the delay rule (a reflection from distance x ripples the spectrum every v divided by 2x) as the course's own working from these, not a quote.

Wirescan injects low-amplitude sine waves, they travel to the far end and reflect back, and the spot signature is an FFT of the input-impedance phase spectrum, which is more sensitive to soft defects with a small impedance change.

DNORM severity is a bar chart of the features that exceed a DNORM threshold setting, colour-coded by severity; the direction (positive or negative) tells the type of impedance change, such as moisture ingress or thermal degradation. The threshold is a software setting (0 dB in one PNNL example), so the colour boundaries have no public numbers.

Test from both ends for the best sensitivity (it is not a necessity); other loads may stay connected if they reflect enough; LIRA suits cables hundreds of kilometres long, which tests at working voltage do not.

Take an initial fingerprint at commissioning; measure at manufacturing milestones, factory acceptance tests, after transport and before, during and after installation; LIRA and TDR fingerprints at FAT, spooling and commissioning generate hundreds of reports, so the data must be kept in a usable form.

Online LIRA exists for energised cables: offline methods are restricted by safety, so the online system uses non-galvanic capacitive and inductive sensors with a band-pass of 100 kHz to 20 MHz; the one case study is a 12/10(24) kV wind-farm cable. No source states a 33 kV limit: the notes' figure stands unconfirmed. String B at 66 kV is tested offline.
Test time: the notes say roughly 1 minute; a Fauske (US distributor) article says about three minutes depending on the cable length.
